title: I Took the Carillon-Clavier Hours to the Carillonneur Who Left My Numbered Pedals

parts.text: I stepped into the tower at 12:03 p.m. and carillonneur Mads was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE CLAVIER. FORTY MINUTES. PEDALS STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-six, tower secretary, holding a clipboard that listed our numbered pedals. Mads shrugged. "Carillonneurs are the tower." I photographed the board, the booking, and his leftover bats on my numbered pedals. Then I asked for the clavier log. At 12:11 the sexton pinged why Mads's name was on my bats. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The sexton can see Mads's leftover bats on my numbered pedals.

social.video_title: He left my numbered carillon pedals on my hours — Part 1/2
social.description: Tower clavier, leftover bats, a forty-minute clock he posted. I logged the pedals. Would you have asked for the clavier log?

parts.text: Mads called it practice peals until the sexton asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the bat still. The pedals went back to my numbered booking. Mads ran a slot of his own and told the next carillonneur atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: CARILLONNEURS ARE NOT THE TOWER. I keep my bats on a labeled peg. Mads brown-bags his peals. The tower finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Carillonneurs are not the tower — Part 2/2
social.description: Clavier log, numbered pedals, and a second line on the board. Was a practice peal ever my bats?
